article_title: The Real Difference Between a Fixed Deposit and a Recurring Deposit
claim: Interest from FDs and RDs is fully taxable as income from other sources, and banks deduct TDS at 10% if interest income from that bank crosses the threshold in a financial year (no specific threshold figure given).
source: Income Tax Act Section 194A as amended by Finance Act 2025 / ClearTax, TaxGarden summaries
required_correction: 10% TDS rate is correct, but the article never states the actual threshold, which changed recently: from FY 2025-26 (w.e.f. 1 Apr 2025) the no-TDS threshold for bank/post-office interest is ₹50,000 for individuals under 60 (raised from ₹40,000) and ₹1,00,000 for senior citizens 60+ (raised from ₹50,000). The article should state these current figures instead of leaving 'the threshold' unspecified.

article_title: The Real Difference Between a Fixed Deposit and a Recurring Deposit
claim: TDS on RD interest works the same way as FD interest (RD interest is subject to TDS under the same provisions).
source: TaxGuru / CharteredClub — Section 194A(3) Explanation 1 amendment (effective 1 June 2015)
required_correction: None — accurate. Recurring deposits were brought within the definition of 'time deposits' under Section 194A(3) effective 1 June 2015, so RD interest is subject to the same 10% TDS and threshold rules as FD interest.

article_title: The Real Difference Between a Fixed Deposit and a Recurring Deposit
claim: Both FD and RD products are backed by DICGC insurance up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank.
source: DICGC (Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation)
required_correction: None — accurate. DICGC cover is ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank (principal + interest combined), raised from ₹1 lakh in February 2020.

article_title: The Real Difference Between a Fixed Deposit and a Recurring Deposit
claim: Premature withdrawal on both FD and RD usually incurs a penalty reduction of 0.5-1% off the applicable rate.
required_correction: This is a commonly cited rule-of-thumb range but penalty rates are bank- and product-specific (e.g. SBI charges 0.50-1% depending on tenure and amount; other banks vary and some charge nothing on short breaks). Article should cite that this varies by bank rather than presenting one universal range, or name specific bank examples with links to their current FD/RD premature withdrawal policy pages.

article_title: The Real Difference Between a Fixed Deposit and a Recurring Deposit
claim: The RD's effective yield is always lower than the quoted rate for the same total money because the average outstanding principal over the year is roughly half of the FD's.
source: Standard RD/FD effective-yield mathematics (compounding on declining average balance)
required_correction: None — the underlying math is correct in direction. The article's editorial note asks that the ₹1,20,000 worked example actually be finished with real maturity numbers; currently it states the concept but never computes the two maturity values, which would make the claim concretely verifiable to the reader rather than asserted.

article_title: The Real Difference Between a Fixed Deposit and a Recurring Deposit
claim: Missing an RD instalment typically triggers a small penalty charge per missed month rather than closing the account, with a grace period before repeated misses force early closure.
source: Bank-specific RD terms (e.g. SBI, HDFC RD missed-instalment policies)
required_correction: Directionally accurate but bank-specific: policies on missed-instalment penalties and grace periods before forced closure vary meaningfully by bank (e.g. number of allowed misses before auto-closure differs). Article should note this varies by bank rather than stating it as a universal rule.

article_title: The Real Difference Between a Fixed Deposit and a Recurring Deposit
claim: A 7% FD in a year with 6% inflation is barely preserving value in real terms.
required_correction: This is a framing/interpretive statement built on a hypothetical, not a specific checkable government or market figure. No correction needed beyond noting it is illustrative, not a current inflation/rate claim.

article_title: How Much of Your Salary Should Actually Go to Rent
claim: The 30% rule was built around gross household income and doesn't account for India-specific deductions like PF, professional tax, and TDS.
required_correction: The origin of the '30% rule' (commonly traced to US housing-affordability guidelines/HUD conventions) is asserted without citation. It's a widely repeated claim but the article should cite where the 30% figure originates rather than stating its provenance as settled fact.

article_title: How Much of Your Salary Should Actually Go to Rent
claim: HRA exemption is the lower of: actual HRA received, rent paid minus 10% of basic salary, or a percentage of basic salary depending on city (implied 50%/40%).
source: Income Tax Act Section 10(13A) read with Rule 2A
required_correction: Correct in substance but should state the exact figures for precision: exemption is the LEAST of (1) actual HRA received, (2) rent paid minus 10% of salary (basic + DA that counts for retirement benefits + turnover-based commission), (3) 50% of salary for Mumbai/Delhi/Kolkata/Chennai or 40% of salary for all other cities. The article names 'a percentage of basic salary depending on city' but never states 50%/40% or which four cities count as metro — this should be made explicit and cite Section 10(13A) / Rule 2A directly.

article_title: How Much of Your Salary Should Actually Go to Rent
claim: The new tax regime doesn't offer the HRA exemption.
source: Section 115BAC, Income Tax Act (new tax regime) / TaxBuddy, ClearTax summaries
required_correction: None — accurate. HRA exemption under Section 10(13A) is not available to taxpayers who opt for the new tax regime under Section 115BAC; HRA received is fully taxable under that regime.

article_title: How Much of Your Salary Should Actually Go to Rent
claim: Take-home pay on a ₹12 lakh CTC is usually around 70-80% of that after PF, professional tax, and TDS.
required_correction: This range is a reasonable rule-of-thumb but is highly dependent on individual CTC structure (bonus/variable pay proportion, employer PF matching, tax regime chosen, HRA and other exemptions claimed) and could not be tied to an authoritative source or standard calculator result. Should be labeled as an illustrative approximation, not a precise statistic, or replaced with a worked example using a stated CTC breakup.

article_title: How Much of Your Salary Should Actually Go to Rent
claim: A ₹25,000 rent might have an effective cost closer to ₹20,000-22,000 once the HRA tax saving is accounted for.
required_correction: This specific illustrative figure depends entirely on the reader's basic salary, HRA component, city, and tax slab, which the article doesn't specify, so the ₹20,000-22,000 range cannot be independently verified as typical. Should either show the underlying assumptions (basic salary, slab rate, city) used to produce this number or clearly flag it as a hypothetical example only.

article_title: How Much of Your Salary Should Actually Go to Rent
claim: Rent as a share of income is structurally higher in Mumbai, Bengaluru, and Delhi-NCR, and someone in Mumbai clearing 40-45% of take-home on rent isn't necessarily reckless.
required_correction: This is an interpretive judgment about what counts as 'reckless' spending, not a checkable statistic. No correction needed; flag as opinion/contextual framing rather than fact.

article_title: How to Read a Loan APR Instead of Just the EMI
claim: RBI requires regulated lenders to provide a Key Fact Statement (KFS) for most retail and personal loans, showing APR, fees, and repayment schedule in a standardized format.
source: RBI Circular RBI/2024-25/18 (Key Facts Statement (KFS) for Loans & Advances), effective 1 October 2024
required_correction: None — accurate. RBI mandated KFS for all new retail and MSME term loans sanctioned on/after 1 October 2024 (circular dated 15 April 2024), requiring standardized disclosure of APR and all charges. Article could strengthen credibility by naming the circular explicitly. Note: KFS does not cover credit cards or non-term MSME lending, a nuance the article omits.

article_title: How to Read a Loan APR Instead of Just the EMI
claim: A reducing balance rate calculates interest only on outstanding principal, while a flat rate calculates interest on the original principal for the whole tenure, making a flat rate loan more expensive than the same headline reducing rate.
source: BankBazaar / DMI Finance — Flat vs Reducing Interest Rate explainers
required_correction: None — mechanically accurate description of how flat-rate and reducing-balance interest are computed.

article_title: How to Read a Loan APR Instead of Just the EMI
claim: Flat-rate loans commonly work out to an effective reducing-rate equivalent of roughly 1.8-2x the stated flat number, depending on tenure; a 13% flat loan is equivalent to roughly 23-24% reducing.
source: BankBazaar / EMI.me flat-vs-reducing rate calculators and industry rule-of-thumb
required_correction: The 1.8-1.9x rule-of-thumb is a widely used approximation for typical 3-5 year tenures, but the exact multiplier is tenure-dependent (shorter tenures produce a smaller gap, longer tenures a larger one) and isn't a fixed, official figure — no RBI or regulatory source publishes a fixed conversion factor. The article's specific '13% flat ≈ 23-24% reducing' example is a plausible but unsourced illustrative calculation; it should show the calculation or cite a specific calculator/example rather than presenting the range as an established constant.

article_title: How to Read a Loan APR Instead of Just the EMI
claim: Processing fees commonly range 0.5-2.5% of the loan amount.
source: CreditMantri, Paisabazaar, DMI Finance personal loan processing fee surveys (2026)
required_correction: Actual market range runs somewhat wider — most sources cite 0.5% to 4% (some up to 5%), with 1-2.5% being the common band for major banks/NBFCs specifically, plus 18% GST charged on top of the fee, which the article never mentions. Update the range to reflect the fuller 0.5-4% spread and add that GST applies on top of the fee.

article_title: How to Read a Loan APR Instead of Just the EMI
claim: Prepayment or foreclosure penalties on some loans commonly run 2-5% of the outstanding principal.
source: HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank personal loan prepayment charge schedules; industry surveys
required_correction: Directionally correct; real-world bank data shows a slightly wider range of roughly 1-6% depending on the bank and how long the loan has run (e.g. HDFC: 4% within 24 EMIs, 3% at 24-36 EMIs, 2% after 36 EMIs; ICICI: 3% within 24 months, 0% after). Article should note that the percentage typically decreases the longer the loan has been running, rather than presenting one flat range.

article_title: How to Read a Loan APR Instead of Just the EMI
claim: Several RBI-regulated loan comparison platforms display APR alongside interest rate.
required_correction: No specific platforms are named, and 'RBI-regulated loan comparison platforms' is an imprecise description — loan aggregator/comparison websites (e.g. BankBazaar, Paisabazaar) are not themselves RBI-regulated entities in the way banks/NBFCs are; they operate as intermediaries. Article should either name specific platforms and clarify their actual regulatory status, or remove the 'RBI-regulated' characterization as currently unsupported.

article_title: How to Read a Loan APR Instead of Just the EMI
claim: Some lenders bundle credit life insurance into a loan, sometimes presented as mandatory when it's optional, inflating the loan principal and interest charged.
source: RBI/consumer-finance reporting on bundled loan insurance practices
required_correction: Directionally accurate and a well-documented practice/complaint area in Indian retail lending; the KFS mandate (Oct 2024) specifically requires insurance charges to be disclosed separately from the loan principal, which the article could cite as the regulatory backstop for this exact issue.

article_title: Remote Work vs Hybrid vs Office: How Each Setup Shapes Your Career Growth
claim: Managers don't promote the person who works hardest — they promote the person whose work they can see and vouch for confidently, and remote work strips out accidental visibility.
required_correction: This is presented as a general mechanism/thesis without any cited survey or study. The editorial note explicitly flags that a real survey citation on remote/hybrid promotion rates would strengthen the piece — none is provided anywhere in the article. Recommend adding a citable data point (e.g. a labor-economics study on remote-worker promotion rates) to move this from assertion to evidence-backed claim.

article_title: Remote Work vs Hybrid vs Office: How Each Setup Shapes Your Career Growth
claim: In informal conversations, many managers admit to a bias that it's easier to advocate for someone whose work they've watched happen in person, even when a remote report's output is comparable or better.
required_correction: No survey, study, or named source is cited for this claim about what managers 'admit privately.' This reads as a plausible but unverifiable generalization presented as established behavior. Should be either sourced to an actual survey (several exist on proximity bias in promotion decisions, e.g. from Future Forum or similar workplace-research groups) or rewritten as an explicitly stated opinion/hypothesis rather than a factual claim about manager behavior.

article_title: Remote Work vs Hybrid vs Office: How Each Setup Shapes Your Career Growth
claim: Most Indian IT and product companies have settled on two-to-three office days a week.
source: Industry hybrid-work policy reporting (e.g. TCS, Infosys, Wipro RTO mandates)
required_correction: Directionally plausible (many large Indian IT firms have moved to 2-3 day RTO mandates through 2024-2026), but no single authoritative industry-wide survey was found confirming 'most' companies specifically settled on 2-3 days as a statistic. Article should cite specific company policies (e.g. TCS's return-to-office stance) rather than asserting an industry-wide average as settled fact.

article_title: Remote Work vs Hybrid vs Office: How Each Setup Shapes Your Career Growth
claim: Early in a career, being in the room matters more because informal, unwritten learning (watching a senior debug live, watching how decisions get made) isn't captured in documentation, and this in-person learning curve flattens out for senior employees.
required_correction: Reasonable, widely-held career advice but not a checkable statistic — presented as interpretation/argument, not fact. No correction needed beyond classification.

article_title: Remote Work vs Hybrid vs Office: How Each Setup Shapes Your Career Growth
claim: A remote employee who asks specific, well-prepared questions in scheduled 1:1s often gets more actual mentorship time than an office employee who's present but never asks.
required_correction: Presented as a general truth but reads as an anecdotal/generic claim with no named source, study, or specific example behind it — has the shape of fabricated-sounding 'often' framing rather than a cited pattern. Should be reframed as the author's opinion/observation rather than an implied fact.

article_title: How to Build a LinkedIn Profile That Recruiters Actually Find
claim: LinkedIn Recruiter lets recruiters search by exact keywords, current title, past titles, skills, location, and school, combined with AND/OR logic (Boolean search).
source: LinkedIn Recruiter Help — Boolean search filters
required_correction: None — accurate. LinkedIn Recruiter supports Boolean (AND/OR/NOT) search across title, location, company, skills, schools, and industries.

article_title: How to Build a LinkedIn Profile That Recruiters Actually Find
claim: LinkedIn's own skill-matching weights skills with the most endorsements more heavily in recruiter search relevance.
required_correction: LinkedIn does not publicly document that endorsement count directly boosts search ranking; this is a commonly repeated claim in LinkedIn-optimization blog content but not confirmed in LinkedIn's own official search/ranking documentation. Should be softened to 'many LinkedIn coaches believe' or removed unless a LinkedIn official source can be found.

article_title: How to Build a LinkedIn Profile That Recruiters Actually Find
claim: LinkedIn's algorithm and many recruiters weight recent activity, and profiles with no updates for over a year rank lower in relevance even with strong keyword coverage.
required_correction: No official LinkedIn documentation or independent study was found confirming a specific 'over a year of inactivity' ranking penalty in recruiter search relevance. This is a plausible but unverified claim commonly repeated in LinkedIn-growth blog content. Should be attributed as anecdotal/industry belief rather than stated as an established platform mechanic.

article_title: How to Build a LinkedIn Profile That Recruiters Actually Find
claim: Profiles without a photo get filtered out or deprioritized in some recruiter searches entirely, since a blank avatar reads as an inactive or fake account.
required_correction: No LinkedIn official source confirms photo-less profiles are algorithmically filtered from search results; LinkedIn does publish general engagement stats favoring profiles with photos, but the specific 'filtered out' claim couldn't be verified. Recommend rewording to the more defensible claim that photo-less profiles receive less recruiter attention/trust, rather than asserting a search-filtering mechanic.

article_title: How to Build a LinkedIn Profile That Recruiters Actually Find
claim: Turning on 'Open to Work' with recruiter-only visibility adds you to a dedicated search pool while staying invisible to your current employer's own recruiters.
source: LinkedIn official Help Center — Open To Work feature
required_correction: None — accurate. LinkedIn's 'Open to Work' feature offers a 'recruiters only' visibility setting specifically designed to signal availability to recruiters using LinkedIn Recruiter while hiding the signal from the user's current company's recruiters/employees, per LinkedIn's own documentation.

article_title: How to Build a LinkedIn Profile That Recruiters Actually Find
claim: The actual job title field under each work experience entry is separately searchable from the headline.
source: LinkedIn Recruiter search filters (title field indexing)
required_correction: None — accurate. LinkedIn Recruiter's 'Job title' filter searches the structured title field on each experience entry, separate from headline text search.

article_title: How to Handle Being Laid Off: The First Two Weeks
claim: Gratuity is included in full and final settlement if the employee has completed five years of service.
source: Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972
required_correction: The five-year rule is correct but incomplete: courts and the Act's 'continuous service' definition recognize an exception where an employee who completes more than 4 years and 240 days in the final year can also qualify, and the five-year requirement is waived entirely in cases of death or disablement. Article should mention the 4-years-240-days exception and the death/disablement waiver, both of which are common real-world scenarios for someone reading a layoff-specific article.

article_title: How to Handle Being Laid Off: The First Two Weeks
claim: India has no automatic health insurance continuation like the US's COBRA — coverage typically ends on the last working day or shortly after if the only cover was the employer's group policy.
source: IRDAI group health insurance / policyholder.gov.in
required_correction: None — accurate. India has no equivalent to COBRA; group employer health cover generally terminates at employment end, and IRDAI portability/migration rules (not automatic continuation) are the mechanism available instead.

article_title: How to Handle Being Laid Off: The First Two Weeks
claim: IRDAI-mandated health insurance portability lets you carry forward credit for waiting periods already served when moving from a group/employer policy to an individual one, or between insurers, as long as there's no gap in coverage.
source: IRDAI — Guidelines on Migration and Portability of Health Insurance Policies / policyholder.gov.in
required_correction: None — accurate in substance. IRDAI's migration/portability regulations allow individual members of a group policy to migrate to an individual/family floater policy with credit for time already served toward waiting periods and pre-existing disease exclusions (capped at 36 months under the 2024 IRDAI Insurance Products Regulations), subject to no break in coverage and (per IRDAI process) intimation to the existing insurer, generally at least 45 days before renewal — a specific procedural detail the article doesn't mention and could usefully add.

article_title: How to Handle Being Laid Off: The First Two Weeks
claim: EPF early withdrawal before five years of continuous service is usually taxable.
source: EPFO / Income Tax Act — EPF withdrawal taxation rules
required_correction: Correct but the article omits a useful specific: TDS on EPF withdrawals under 5 years' service only applies if the withdrawal exceeds ₹50,000 (10% TDS with PAN, 20% without; avoidable via Form 15G/15H if income is below the taxable threshold), a Finance Act 2016 provision effective since 1 June 2016. Adding this threshold and the Form 15G/15H workaround would make the section concretely actionable rather than a general caution.

article_title: How to Handle Being Laid Off: The First Two Weeks
claim: EPF left inactive keeps earning interest for a few years even if inactive.
source: EPFO rules on inoperative accounts
required_correction: This is true only up to a point and stated too loosely: EPFO pays interest on inoperative accounts, but an account becomes 'inoperative' (and interest treatment/tax status can change) if no contribution is received for 36 months after retirement/permanent departure from employment, and interest earned after that point becomes taxable in the depositor's hands. The article's 'a few years' phrasing without the 36-month rule and its tax consequence could leave readers assuming indefinite risk-free accrual.

article_title: How to Handle Being Laid Off: The First Two Weeks
claim: Vested ESOPs commonly must be exercised within 90 days of the last working day or they're forfeited.
source: Qapita, Carta, Hissa — Post-Termination Exercise Period (PTEP) explainers for Indian startups
required_correction: 90 days is a commonly cited standard/default in Indian startup ESOP plans, but there is no single legal mandate fixing this figure — the actual window is governed entirely by each company's specific ESOP plan document, and ranges from 30 days to several years (some progressive startups now offer 1-10 years). Article should clarify that 90 days is a common default, not a fixed rule, and tell the reader to check their own ESOP/plan agreement rather than assume 90 days applies.

article_title: How to Handle Being Laid Off: The First Two Weeks
claim: Pausing a running SIP rather than cancelling it preserves the account and accumulated units, and most mutual fund platforms allow a pause without penalty, unlike a full redemption which can trigger exit loads or tax implications.
source: AMFI / mutual fund platform SIP pause policies
required_correction: Directionally accurate — SIP pause facilities exist on most major platforms and redemption can trigger exit loads (typically within 1 year, commonly ~1%) and capital gains tax, while pausing does not. However 'most platforms allow a pause without penalty' could not be confirmed as a universal figure since pause features, duration limits, and eligibility vary by AMC/platform (e.g. some cap pause duration at 1-3 months). Recommend naming specific platform examples or softening 'most' to reflect this variability.

article_title: How to Handle Being Laid Off: The First Two Weeks
claim: India doesn't have a broad unemployment insurance system most private-sector employees can draw on, though a few states/industries have limited schemes.
source: Atal Bimit Vyakti Kalyan Yojana (ABVKY) under ESIC — limited unemployment benefit scheme
required_correction: Accurate at a general level. One specific scheme the article could name to make 'limited schemes' concrete: the Atal Bimit Vyakti Kalyan Yojana under ESIC, which provides limited cash relief to ESI-covered private-sector employees who lose their jobs involuntarily — but coverage is restricted to ESI-registered employees (broadly lower-wage formal-sector workers), so it does not apply to most white-collar salaried employees, consistent with the article's overall point.

article_title: How to Link Aadhaar and PAN Online — Step by Step
claim: The late-linking fee is ₹1,000, paid through e-Pay Tax on the income tax portal, selecting the relevant assessment year and 'Other Receipts' as payment type.
source: Income Tax Department — Link Aadhaar FAQ (incometax.gov.in)
required_correction: Fee amount confirmed at ₹1,000. Minor correction: the official payment type/minor head is specifically listed as 'Fee for delay in linking PAN with Aadhaar' under Section 234H (some references list it under 'Other Receipts (500)/Fee' category on the e-Pay Tax flow) — article should double check and match the exact current dropdown wording on the live e-Pay Tax page, since portal UI labels can shift and this is exactly the kind of concrete step-by-step detail the editorial note flags as needing a 'last verified' date.

article_title: How to Link Aadhaar and PAN Online — Step by Step
claim: A small category of PAN holders are exempt from linking: residents of Assam, Jammu & Kashmir, and Meghalaya, NRIs per the Income Tax Act, and individuals above a certain age at the time the rule was introduced.
source: Income Tax Department — Link Aadhaar FAQ (incometax.gov.in)
required_correction: Confirmed but the article should state the exact age threshold instead of the vague 'above a certain age': the exemption applies to individuals aged 80 years or above during the previous year (super senior citizens), plus non-citizens of India as a fourth category the article omits entirely.

article_title: How to Link Aadhaar and PAN Online — Step by Step
claim: An OTP for the Link Aadhaar request goes to the mobile number registered with Aadhaar, not the one registered with bank or PAN.
source: Income Tax Department e-filing portal — Link Aadhaar process
required_correction: None — accurate. The OTP verification step in the Link Aadhaar flow is sent to the mobile number linked to the Aadhaar record via UIDAI, which can differ from the number linked to a bank account or PAN profile.

article_title: How to Link Aadhaar and PAN Online — Step by Step
claim: If TDS was deducted at a higher rate during a period the PAN was inoperative, the excess can usually be claimed back as a refund when filing the return for that year, once the PAN becomes operative and the correction falls within the same or adjoining assessment years.
source: Income Tax Department — Section 206AA / CBDT Circular on inoperative PAN and higher TDS
required_correction: Directionally correct in that becoming PAN-operative again generally allows normal TDS credit reconciliation going forward, but the specific claim about reclaiming already-deducted higher-rate TDS via refund, and the 'same or adjoining assessment years' caveat, is a nuanced area that has seen CBDT circulars/clarifications change over time (e.g. CBDT Circular 6/2024 gave relief for certain transactions if PAN-Aadhaar was linked by specific deadlines). Article should cite the specific CBDT circular governing this relief rather than stating the mechanism generically, since the exact conditions for reclaiming already-deducted higher TDS are more restrictive and technical than 'file your return and it gets reconciled.'

article_title: How to Link Aadhaar and PAN Online — Step by Step
claim: An inoperative PAN blocks opening a new bank account, demat account, or mutual fund folio, and in some cases blocks KYC refresh on an existing account.
source: Income Tax Department — consequences of inoperative PAN (Section 206AA/206CC linked FAQ)
required_correction: None — accurate. Official consequences of an inoperative PAN include higher TDS/TCS deduction, withheld refunds, and loss of interest on refunds; financial institutions independently require an operative PAN for KYC on new accounts/folios per PAN validation requirements, consistent with the article's description.

article_title: How to Link Aadhaar and PAN Online — Step by Step
claim: Once linking is confirmed, the status page shows 'Aadhaar-PAN linking is completed successfully,' and a formal downloadable acknowledgment with a reference number is available under the same Link Aadhaar Status section.
source: Income Tax Department e-filing portal — Link Aadhaar Status page
required_correction: The general flow (status check, confirmation message, downloadable acknowledgment) is consistent with how the portal operates, but exact UI wording and whether a separate downloadable acknowledgment (vs. just a status message) is available can change with portal updates. Given the article's own editorial note calling for screenshots and a 'last verified' date, this step-by-step UI claim should be re-confirmed against the live portal immediately before publish and dated.
